title: The digital revolution
summary: In 1945 John von Neumann outlined the architecture of a stored-program computer in a widely circulated paper. ENIAC, announced on February 14, 1946 at the University of Pennsylvania, was the first general-purpose electronic computer. The transistor, microprocessor, Internet and World Wide Web, all with their own records, followed.

uncertainty.note: ENIAC was completed and ran its first test computations in late 1945 at Penn; von Neumann's First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC was distributed in June 1945.

as_recorded.value: In a widely circulated paper, mathematician John von Neumann outlines the architecture of a stored-program computer

where.modern_name: Worldwide; stand-in pin at Philadelphia, United States

importance.justification: The transition to digital electronics and stored-program computing transformed global industry, information processing, and modern daily life.

related.because: The rise of electronic digital computers created the demand and hardware basis for interconnected packet-switched computer networks.
General-purpose digital computers enabled research into networking protocols across distant computing centers.

sources.title: Celebrating Penn Engineering History: ENIAC
sources.publisher: University of Pennsylvania School of Engineering and Applied Science
sources.author: Penn Engineering

reviewer_note: There is no agreed start date. The sources cover its beginnings, not its wider effects on society. The pin marks ENIAC in Philadelphia, and the change itself is worldwide.
